a: who has a fire in Zion / and a furnace in Jerusalem
t: A fire in Zion, or offspring?
p: The Greek ends the chapter with a blessing: happy is the one who has offspring in Zion and family in Jerusalem.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); KJV
readings.orig: אֲשֶׁר־אוּר לוֹ בְּצִיּוֹן וְתַנּוּר לוֹ בִּירוּשָׁלָםִ
readings.en: whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem
readings.plain: who has a fire in Zion / and a furnace in Jerusalem

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete)
readings.orig: μακάριος ὃς ἔχει ἐν Σειὼν σπέρμα καὶ οἰκείους ἐν Ἰερουσαλήμ
readings.en: happy is he who has seed in Zion and household in Jerusalem
readings.plain: and happy is the one who has offspring in Zion / and family in Jerusalem

why: The Hebrew witnesses agree. The Greek translator seems to have read or heard different words for "fire" and "furnace," and turned the threat into a blessing on Zion's families. The Plain follows the Hebrew, which fits the fire imagery of 29:6, 30:27–33 and 33:14.

a: his heart works at wickedness
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll says the fool's heart 'plans' evil, and the Greek also has a verb of thinking.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV ("his heart will work iniquity")
readings.plain: his heart works at wickedness

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); compare the Septuagint ("his heart will think vain things")
readings.plain: his heart plans wickedness

why: "Plans" is the more usual verb with "heart" (Psalm 36:4; Micah 2:1), so it could be a scribe's smoothing of the harder "does." The sense hardly changes. The Plain keeps the Masoretic Text.

a: Be their arm
p: The Hebrew says 'their arm' in a prayer that otherwise says 'us'. The Latin and many modern versions say 'our arm'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); 4Q57 (4QIsa-c); KJV ("be thou their arm")
readings.plain: Be their arm

readings.w: Latin Vulgate; many modern translations
readings.plain: Be our arm

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete), reading the same letters as zera', "seed"
readings.orig: ἐγενήθη τὸ σπέρμα τῶν ἀπειθούντων εἰς ἀπώλειαν
readings.en: the seed of the disobedient has come to ruin
readings.plain: Let the offspring of the disobedient come to ruin

why: Every Hebrew witness, including two scrolls from Qumran, has "their arm." The shift from "us" to "their" may mean the prophet prays for the people, or the soldiers who defend them. "Our" is the easier reading and is probably a translator's smoothing.

a: cities spurned
p: The Masoretic Text says 'cities'. The Great Isaiah Scroll says 'witnesses', a closer match to a broken covenant.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4Q57 (4QIsa-c); KJV ("he hath despised the cities")
readings.plain: cities spurned

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); preferred by many commentators
readings.plain: witnesses spurned

why: Hebrew r and d look almost alike. "Witnesses" fits the line about a broken covenant, since treaties were sworn before witnesses, and many scholars prefer it. But 4Q57, another scroll from Qumran, agrees with the Masoretic Text, and Sennacherib's taking of Judah's walled towns gives "cities" good sense too. The Plain keeps the Masoretic Text.

a: The whole army of heaven will rot
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll begins the verse with 'the valleys will split open' and has the stars 'fall' rather than 'rot'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV ("all the host of heaven shall be dissolved")
readings.en: and all the army of heaven will rot
readings.plain: The whole army of heaven will rot

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.orig: והעמקים יתבקעו וכול צבא השמים יפולו
readings.en: and the valleys will split, and all the army of heaven will fall
readings.plain: The valleys will split open, and the whole army of heaven will fall

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete)
readings.orig: καὶ τακήσονται πᾶσαι αἱ δυνάμεις τῶν οὐρανῶν
readings.en: and all the powers of the heavens will melt
readings.plain: All the powers of heaven will melt

why: The scroll's extra line echoes Micah 1:4, where the valleys split apart, and "fall" matches the falling leaves later in the verse. Both look like a scribe's expansion from other passages. The Greek "melt" supports the Masoretic "rot," though the Greek also says that "all the stars will fall," like the scroll and Revelation 6:13. The Plain keeps the Masoretic Text.

a: my sword has drunk deep in the heavens
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll says the sword 'will appear' in the heavens instead of having 'drunk deep' there.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Septuagint ("my sword has become drunk in heaven"); KJV ("my sword shall be bathed in heaven")
readings.en: for my sword has drunk its fill in the heavens
readings.plain: my sword has drunk deep in the heavens

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: for my sword will appear in the heavens
readings.plain: my sword will appear in the heavens

why: The two verbs share letters (rwth and tr'h). "Has drunk deep" is the harder picture, and it is supported by the Greek and by 34:7, which uses the same verb: "Their land will drink deep of blood." The scroll may have softened it. The Plain keeps the Masoretic Text.

a: Lilith
p: The Masoretic Text has 'Lilith' in the singular; the Great Isaiah Scroll has a plural, 'liliths'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: Lilith

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.plain: Liliths

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete)
readings.plain: Donkey-centaurs

readings.w: Latin Vulgate
readings.plain: The lamia

readings.w: KJV
readings.plain: The screech owl

why: The scroll's plural fits the plural verbs it uses in the rest of the line, and it treats liliths as a class of creatures, as the Songs of the Sage from Qumran also do. The Masoretic singular names one figure. The translations show how early readers struggled with the word; see the note.

a: my mouth
p: The Masoretic Text has 'my mouth', with God or the prophet speaking. The Great Isaiah Scroll has 'his mouth'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV ("for my mouth it hath commanded")
readings.plain: my mouth

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); compare the Septuagint ("for the Lord commanded them")
readings.plain: his mouth

why: "His mouth" matches "his spirit" in the next line and "the LORD's scroll" before it, and many scholars prefer it. But it is also the easier reading. In "my mouth" the prophet's voice and God's run together, as often in Isaiah. The Plain keeps the Masoretic Text.

a: I say: a plan and strength for war are mere words from your lips.
p: Isaiah's Masoretic Text has 'I say'. Kings and the Great Isaiah Scroll have 'you say', which changes the sentence.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV ("I say, sayest thou...")
readings.en: I said: only a word of lips, counsel and strength for war
readings.plain: I say: a plan and strength for war are mere words from your lips.

readings.w: 2 Kings 18:20 (Masoretic Text); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.plain: Do you think mere words from your lips make a plan and strength for war?

why: The two forms differ by one letter at the end. With "I say," the Rabshakeh gives his own verdict on Hezekiah's war plans; with "you say," he mocks Hezekiah's claim. Either way the point is the same. The Plain follows Isaiah's Masoretic Text here and the Kings Plain elsewhere in the speech.

a: in front of this altar.
p: Kings and the Great Isaiah Scroll end with 'this altar in Jerusalem'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: before this altar you must bow down
readings.plain: in front of this altar.

readings.w: 2 Kings 18:22 (Masoretic Text); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.plain: in front of this altar in Jerusalem.

why: The Hebrew "this altar" already means the temple altar in Jerusalem, so the words add nothing new. The scroll may have filled in from Kings, or Isaiah's text may have lost them. The scroll also makes "you tell me" plural, as if speaking to the people. The Greek of Isaiah stops after "We trust in the Lord our God." The Plain keeps Isaiah's Masoretic Text.

a: eat their own dung and drink their own urine
p: As in 2 Kings 18:27, the written Hebrew has crude words, and the Masoretes marked politer ones to be read aloud.

readings.w: Masoretic written text (Ketiv); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC), which writes the crude words in the text; KJV
readings.plain: eat their own dung and drink their own urine

readings.w: Masoretic reading tradition (Qere)
readings.en: their excrement ... the water of their feet
readings.plain: eat their own excrement and drink the water of their own feet

why: The question is how to read the verse aloud, not what the soldier said; see the variant on 2 Kings 18:27. The Great Isaiah Scroll shows that some copyists simply wrote the blunt words.

a: for he cannot rescue you.
p: Kings adds 'from his hand'. The Great Isaiah Scroll instead reads 'the king of Assyria says'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Septuagint (Swete)
readings.plain: for he cannot rescue you.

readings.w: 2 Kings 18:29 (Masoretic Text)
readings.plain: for he cannot rescue you from his hand.

why: In Kings, "his hand" is awkward, since the Assyrian king is the speaker, and the Greek and Latin of Kings read "my hand." Isaiah's shorter text avoids the problem. The Great Isaiah Scroll also names "the king of Assyria" in place of "the king" at the start of the verse.

a: a land of bread and vineyards.
p: Kings goes on: 'a land of olive oil and honey. Live, and don't die!' Isaiah stops at bread and vineyards.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); Septuagint (Swete)
readings.en: a land of bread and vineyards
readings.plain: a land of bread and vineyards.

readings.w: 2 Kings 18:32 (Masoretic Text)
readings.orig: ... אֶרֶץ זֵית יִצְהָר וּדְבַשׁ וִחְיוּ וְלֹא תָמֻתוּ
readings.en: ... a land of olive oil and honey; live and do not die
readings.plain: a land of bread and vineyards, a land of olive oil and honey. Live, and don't die!

why: All the witnesses of Isaiah have the shorter text. Kings' extra lines echo Deuteronomy 8:8 and 30:19. Whether Isaiah shortened or Kings expanded is part of the larger question of which book came first; see the note on 36:1.

a: Where are the gods of Sepharvaim?
p: Kings adds 'Hena and Ivvah' to Sepharvaim. Isaiah lists them only in the letter at 37:13.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); Septuagint ("the god of the city of Sepharvaim")
readings.en: where are the gods of Sepharvaim
readings.plain: Where are the gods of Sepharvaim?

readings.w: 2 Kings 18:34 (Masoretic Text)
readings.plain: Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena and Ivvah?

why: The two names may have come into Kings from 2 Kings 19:13 (Isaiah 37:13). All witnesses to Isaiah lack them here.

a: When he heard it, he sent messengers
p: Isaiah says 'he heard and sent', Kings 'he again sent'. The Great Isaiah Scroll and the Greek have both verbs.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV ("when he heard it, he sent messengers")
readings.en: and he heard, and he sent
readings.plain: When he heard it, he sent messengers

readings.w: 2 Kings 19:9 (Masoretic Text)
readings.plain: So he once more sent messengers

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); Septuagint ("and hearing, he turned back and sent")
readings.en: and he heard, and again sent
readings.plain: When he heard it, he once more sent messengers

why: Wayyishma' (heard) and wayyashov (returned, again) look alike. The scroll's double reading may combine the two forms, or may be the original that each book shortened. The Plain keeps Isaiah's Masoretic Text, which makes sense on its own: the news of Tirhakah's march spurs a second message.

a: that you are the LORD, you alone.
t: The LORD alone, or God alone?
p: Isaiah's Masoretic Text reads 'you are the LORD, you alone'. Kings, the Great Isaiah Scroll and the Greek have 'God'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV ("that thou art the LORD, even thou only")
readings.en: that you are the LORD by yourself
readings.plain: that you are the LORD, you alone.

readings.w: 2 Kings 19:19 (Masoretic Text); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); Septuagint ("that you are God alone")
readings.en: that you, LORD, are God alone
readings.plain: that you, LORD, are God, and only you.

why: The other witnesses all have "God," and Isaiah's Masoretic Text may have lost the word. But "you are the LORD" is the confession of Isaiah 40–55 (42:8; 45:5–6, 18), and the shorter reading makes good sense. The Plain keeps it and notes the other.

a: Through your servants
p: Isaiah has 'your servants', Kings 'your messengers'. The Greek of Isaiah agrees with Kings.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); KJV
readings.en: by the hand of your servants
readings.plain: Through your servants

readings.w: 2 Kings 19:23 (Masoretic Text); Septuagint of Isaiah ("through messengers")
readings.en: by the hand of your messengers
readings.plain: Through your messengers

why: Both mean the Rabshakeh and his fellow envoys. The Hebrew of Isaiah is supported by the Qumran scroll; the Greek translator may have known the Kings form.

a: I reached its farthest height
p: Isaiah reads 'its farthest height'; Kings has 'its farthest lodge'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); KJV ("the height of his border")
readings.plain: I reached its farthest height

readings.w: 2 Kings 19:23 (Masoretic Text)
readings.en: the lodging place at its end
readings.plain: I reached its farthest lodge

why: Marom (height) may have come from "mountain heights" earlier in the verse, or malon (lodge) may be the original. The difference is small.

a: I drank water.
p: Kings and the Great Isaiah Scroll have 'strange (foreign) water'. Isaiah's Masoretic Text has only 'water'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV ("I have digged, and drunk water")
readings.plain: I drank water.

readings.w: 2 Kings 19:24 (Masoretic Text); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.plain: I drank the water of strange lands.

why: The point of the boast is that Sennacherib drank from wells he dug in foreign lands, so "strange" may have dropped out of Isaiah's text. But the shorter line still makes sense, and the Plain follows Isaiah's Masoretic Text. The Greek of Isaiah differs widely ("I set a bridge and dried up waters").

a: dried up before it can stand tall
p: Isaiah's Hebrew reads 'a field'; Kings, 'scorched'; the Great Isaiah Scroll, 'scorched before the east wind'.

readings.w: Isaiah: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and a field (terrace) before standing grain
readings.plain: a field before the grain stands up

readings.w: 2 Kings 19:26 (Masoretic Text); KJV ("as corn blasted before it be grown up")
readings.plain: dried up before it can stand tall

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.plain: scorched before the east wind

why: Shedemah (field) and shedefah (scorching) differ by one letter. "Scorched" fits grass on the rooftops, and the Great Isaiah Scroll, though it differs again, supports it. Here the Plain follows Kings and keeps the Kings Plain line; this is the one place in 36–39 where it leaves Isaiah's Masoretic Text. See the variant on 2 Kings 19:26.

a: I know when you sit down
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll adds 'your rising' before 'your sitting', as in Psalm 139:2.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 2 Kings 19:27; Septuagint; KJV
readings.plain: I know when you sit down

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.plain: I know when you rise up, when you sit down

why: The scroll's form matches the pairs "go out" and "come in," and Psalm 139:2: "You yourself know my sitting down and my getting up." A scribe could have added it to complete the pair. All other witnesses lack it.

a: The angel of the LORD went out
p: Kings begins: 'It happened that night.' Isaiah's witnesses lack the words.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); Septuagint
readings.en: and the angel of the LORD went out
readings.plain: The angel of the LORD went out

readings.w: 2 Kings 19:35 (Masoretic Text)
readings.en: and it happened that night, and he went out
readings.plain: It happened that night. The angel of the LORD went out

why: In Kings the words tie the angel's blow to the night after Isaiah's oracle. Isaiah's form leaves the time open; the dead are found "early in the morning."

a: I will cover this city like a shield.
p: Kings and the Great Isaiah Scroll add 'for my own sake and for David my servant's sake'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Septuagint (Swete); KJV
readings.en: and I will shield this city
readings.plain: I will cover this city like a shield.

readings.w: 2 Kings 20:6 (Masoretic Text); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: ... for my sake and for the sake of David my servant
readings.plain: I will cover this city like a shield, for my own sake and for David my servant's sake.

why: The words also close 37:35, so they may have been copied here from there or from Kings. The Plain keeps the shorter Masoretic Text of Isaiah.

a: on the steps of Ahaz
t: The steps of Ahaz's upper room
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads 'the steps of the upper room of Ahaz'; the Greek, 'the steps of your father's house'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV ("the sun dial of Ahaz")
readings.plain: on the steps of Ahaz

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: on the steps of the upper room of Ahaz
readings.plain: on the steps of the upper room of Ahaz

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete)
readings.orig: τοὺς δέκα ἀναβαθμοὺς τοῦ οἴκου τοῦ πατρός σου
readings.en: the ten steps of your father's house
readings.plain: on the steps of your father's house

why: The scroll's "upper room" ('aliyyah) recalls "the upper room of Ahaz" whose altars Josiah tore down (2 Kings 23:12), and suggests a stairway to a roof chamber. The Greek avoids naming Ahaz. The Plain keeps the Masoretic Text; the KJV's "sun dial" is an interpretation.

a: A writing
t: A writing, a miktam, or a prayer?
p: Hebrew miktav, 'a writing', is often emended to miktam, a psalm-title word. The Greek has 'prayer'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); KJV
readings.plain: A writing

readings.w: A common emendation (compare Psalms 16 and 56–60)
readings.plain: A miktam

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete)
readings.plain: A prayer

why: All the Hebrew witnesses have miktav. Miktam fits a psalm title, but no manuscript reads it. The Plain keeps the attested word.

a: Isaiah said, "Let them take a lump of pressed figs and rub it on the sore, so that he may live."
t: Added later in the Great Isaiah Scroll
p: The first copyist of the Great Isaiah Scroll lacked 38:21–22, and another hand added them. Goes with 38:22.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC), as corrected; 1Q8 (1QIsa-b); Septuagint ("Isaiah said to Hezekiah")
readings.en: Isaiah said, Let them take a cake of figs
readings.plain: Isaiah said, "Let them take a lump of pressed figs and rub it on the sore, so that he may live."

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC), first hand

why: Every other witness has the verse, including 1Q8, the second Isaiah scroll from the same cave. Whether the first copy of 1QIsa-a shows an older, shorter Isaiah or an accidental skip is debated; see the note on 38:21.

a: And Hezekiah said, "What is the sign that I will go up to the LORD's house?"
t: Added later in the Great Isaiah Scroll
p: Like 38:21, this verse was missing from the first copy of the Great Isaiah Scroll and was added by another hand.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC), as corrected; 1Q8 (1QIsa-b); Septuagint
readings.en: Hezekiah said, What is the sign
readings.plain: And Hezekiah said, "What is the sign that I will go up to the LORD's house?"

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC), first hand

why: Both 38:20 and 38:22 end with "the LORD's house," so a copyist's eye could easily skip from one to the other. See the note on 38:21.

a: and had gotten well
p: Isaiah adds that Hezekiah 'had recovered'; Kings says only that he had been sick.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 1Q8; KJV ("and was recovered")
readings.plain: and had gotten well

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.plain: and had lived

readings.w: 2 Kings 20:12 (Masoretic Text)

why: The words make the link to chapter 38 plain. The Great Isaiah Scroll uses the verb "live" of 38:1, 9 and 21. The scroll 4Q56 also reads "for he had heard," as 2 Kings 20:12 does, where the Masoretic Text of Isaiah has "and he heard." The Plain keeps the Masoretic Text.

a: Hezekiah was glad to see them
p: Isaiah has 'was glad', Kings 'listened to them'. See the variant on 2 Kings 20:13.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); 1Q8; 4Q56; Septuagint (ἐχάρη); KJV ("was glad of them")
readings.plain: Hezekiah was glad to see them

readings.w: 2 Kings 20:13 (Masoretic Text)
readings.plain: Hezekiah listened to them

why: All witnesses to Isaiah agree. The Plain follows each book's own Hebrew.

a: For there will be peace and safety in my days.
p: Isaiah reads 'For there will be peace'; Kings asks 'Is it not good, if...?' The Greek turns it into a wish.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); 1Q8; 4Q56; KJV ("For there shall be peace and truth in my days")
readings.en: for there will be peace and truth in my days
readings.plain: For there will be peace and safety in my days.

readings.w: 2 Kings 20:19 (Masoretic Text)
readings.en: is it not good, if there will be peace and truth in my days
readings.plain: Is it not good, if there will be peace and safety in my days?

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete)
readings.orig: γενέσθω δὴ εἰρήνη καὶ δικαιοσύνη ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις μου
readings.en: let there be peace and righteousness in my days
readings.plain: Let there be peace and righteousness in my days.

why: All the Hebrew witnesses to Isaiah read the statement. The Plain follows them; see the note.

a: a haunt of ostriches.
p: The Masoretic Text has chatsir, 'haunt' (or 'grass'); the Great Isaiah Scroll spells chatser, 'court, enclosure'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: a haunt of ostriches.

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.plain: a court for ostriches.

why: Chatsir usually means "grass," but here, beside "den," it is best taken as a second word meaning "abode, haunt" (compare 35:7). The scroll's spelling makes it "court," the reading the KJV also gives. The difference is one vowel letter, and the sense is close.

a: Don't talk to us in Judean while the people on the wall are listening.
t: "These words" to "the men on the wall"
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll says 'do not speak these words in the hearing of the men sitting on the wall'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 2 Kings 18:26; KJV
readings.orig: וְאַל־תְּדַבֵּר אֵלֵינוּ יְהוּדִית בְּאָזְנֵי הָעָם אֲשֶׁר עַל־הַחוֹמָה
readings.en: and do not speak to us in Judean in the ears of the people who are on the wall
readings.plain: Don't talk to us in Judean while the people on the wall are listening.

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.orig: ואל תדבר את הדברים האלה באוזני האנשים היושבים על החומה
readings.en: and do not speak these words in the ears of the men sitting on the wall
readings.plain: Don't speak these words while the men sitting on the wall are listening.

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete)
readings.orig: καὶ μὴ λάλει πρὸς ἡμᾶς Ἰουδαιστί· καὶ ἵνα τί λαλεῖς εἰς τὰ ὦτα τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐπὶ τῷ τείχει
readings.en: and do not speak to us in Judean; and why do you speak in the ears of the men on the wall?
readings.plain: Don't talk to us in Judean. Why speak where the men on the wall can hear?

why: The scroll's "the men sitting on the wall" matches the Rabshakeh's reply in 36:12, and may have been drawn from it; it also drops "to us in Judean." The Greek has "men" too. The Plain keeps the Masoretic Text, which agrees with Kings.

a: all the lands and their territory
p: Isaiah: 'all the lands and their land'; the Great Isaiah Scroll: 'all the lands'; Kings: 'the nations and their lands'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Septuagint ("the whole inhabited world and their land")
readings.en: all the lands and their land
readings.plain: all the lands and their territory

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.plain: all the lands

readings.w: 2 Kings 19:17 (Masoretic Text)
readings.plain: the nations and their lands

why: Kings makes the best sense, and Isaiah's "lands" may have come in from 37:11. The scroll's shorter text may be a copyist's way of removing the awkward phrase. The Greek supports the Masoretic Text. The Plain keeps it, rendering the second "land" as "territory."
